title: Thumbelina

full_text:
Once upon a time, a lonely woman who longed for a little child sought counsel from a wise old woman. The old woman gave her a magic barleycorn, saying: "Plant this in a flowerpot, and watch what blossoms."

The woman planted the grain, and immediately a splendid red tulip shot up. Inside the closed petals sat a tiny, delicate maiden, no longer than a person's thumb. She was named Thumbelina. Her cradle was a polished walnut shell, her mattress was blue violet petals, and her counterpane was a fragrant rose leaf.

One night, an ugly, slimy toad hopped through a broken windowpane and carried off Thumbelina's walnut cradle to the marshy riverbank. "Croak, croak, brek-ek-kex!" rasped the old toad, planning to marry the tiny maiden to her clumsy son. They placed Thumbelina on a broad water-lily leaf in the middle of the stream so she could not escape. Thumbelina wept bitter tears of sorrow.

Hearing her cries, the little fish swimming beneath the water resolved that so sweet a child must never marry an ugly toad. They nibbled through the green stalk of the water-lily pad, and the leaf floated freely down the sparkling river, carrying Thumbelina away through sunshine and dancing butterflies.

Summer passed happily as Thumbelina lived in the great forest, drinking nectar from clover and sleeping under a broad burdock leaf. But when bitter winter arrived, the green leaves withered, snow fell in heavy flakes, and Thumbelina shivered in the freezing blast.

Numb with cold, she stumbled upon the underground burrow of an old field mouse. The kindly field mouse took pity on the shivering girl: "Come into my warm room, eat a grain of corn, and tell me stories through the long winter."

In the dark subterranean tunnels lived their neighbor, a wealthy mole dressed in black velvet who despised the sun and flowers. In the passage, Thumbelina discovered a swallow lying motionless, frozen by the sudden frost. The mole kicked the bird contemptuously, but Thumbelina's heart ached with tenderness. That night, she wove a blanket of soft hay, covered the cold swallow, and pressed her cheek against its chest. To her astonishment, she felt a faint, slow heartbeat! The swallow was not dead, only numbed by the bitter chill.

All winter, Thumbelina secretly tended the bird with warm water and soft moss. When spring's golden sun returned, the swallow revived, thanked his little savior with joyful chirps, and flew up into the open sky.

Soon, the field mouse announced that Thumbelina must marry the blind mole and live forever underground in the sunless earth. Thumbelina wept, begging to step into the daylight one last time to bid farewell to the radiant sun.

Suddenly, she heard a sweet twit-twit overhead. It was her beloved swallow! "The cruel winter is over," sang the bird. "Climb onto my back, dear Thumbelina, and let me carry you over mountain and sea to sunny southern lands!"

Thumbelina gladly mounted the swallow's feather back. They soared high above snow-capped peaks and azure oceans until they arrived in a paradise of blooming myrtle and marble palaces. The swallow placed Thumbelina upon a white blossom. In the center of the flower sat a tiny prince with a golden crown and translucent wings—the King of the Flower Spirits!

The prince fell instantly in love with Thumbelina's gentleness, placed his golden crown upon her head, and gave her a pair of delicate wings so she could fly from blossom to blossom in eternal sunshine and joy.
moral: Gentleness of heart and kindness to the helpless guide us through dark trials toward true belonging and light.
